quotes.text: Managed Payments calculates tax based on volume and sales thresholds in each jurisdiction, which can result in transactions with `taxability_reason: not_subject_to_tax` in supported countries.
Managed Payments still handles indirect tax compliance for these transactions.
with no additional charge for Stripe Tax calculation fees on Managed Payments transactions.
You can still use Managed Payments as the merchant of record on these transactions to manage payments, fraud prevention, disputes, and customer support.
These invoices use your business name and tax details, instead of *Sold through Link, LLC*.

findings: Both captures describe Managed Payments assuming responsibility for sales tax, VAT and GST on qualifying sales of digital products in covered domestic and cross-border locations. Where required Stripe calculates/collects tax, registers, files and remits, and issues tax invoices. Both retain the Singapore and Japan domestic exceptions, unchanged cross-border destination lists, and the Serbia VAT-registration restriction (old raw lines 8-131 and new raw lines 9-134).

Where the seller owns indirect-tax compliance the merchant can retain the Managed Payments merchant-of-record and operations arrangement. Stripe Tax can help track thresholds and calculate and collect after the seller supplies registration, with optional registration/filing/remittance partners. Managed Payments still sends a seller-identified invoice and Link-branded receipt email/PDF (old raw lines 133-157, new raw lines 136-161).

Purely presentation edits are the buyer-to-customer terminology in the Singapore sentence, trailing whitespace, Markdown numbering/spacing and italics (diff lines 9-17 and 19-36). The cross-border list and Dashboard navigation do not change, and no scope change follows the buyer/customer vocabulary difference.

Root wiki index line 7 leads to Stripe index lines 130-135, 788 and 792. Managed Payments concept lines 48-58 and 113-118 already route the topic. substantive_changes: The November 7 page newly explains threshold-based calculation by jurisdiction, a possible supported-transaction `taxability_reason: not_subject_to_tax`, and that Managed Payments still handles indirect-tax compliance for those transactions. The April 23 section goes straight from covered digital-product sales to domestic exceptions (old raw lines 19-25; new raw lines 20-28; diff lines 3-9). This is new substantive documentation about responsibility under a particular outcome, without evidence of a newly deployed feature, a new field or changed thresholds.
historical_claims_to_preserve: Preserve the April 23, 2026 capture date recorded at old raw line 2, its country lists and conditions, the domestic and Serbia exceptions, seller responsibility in unsupported tax cases, optional Stripe Tax and exact fee scope and distinct invoice/receipt claims (old raw lines 8-157). The November addition only establishes its own dated threshold/reason statement.

Preserve Dashboard registration upload and partner-assistance routes (old raw lines 141-151, new raw lines 144-155). Neither confers tax status or proves the seller or any specific customer is eligible for Managed Payments.
conflicts: Current source lines 13 and 15-22 and Managed Payments concept lines 10, 54, 64 and 107 use broad automatic-compliance phrasing. Limit it to indirect taxes on covered digital-product sales and to where required. The new `taxability_reason: not_subject_to_tax` example is compatible with continued Managed Payments responsibility in a supported jurisdiction. It does not say that a country lost coverage, that the seller must take over, or that every zero-tax result carries that reason (old raw lines 8-25, new raw lines 9-28).

Current source lines 55-73 and the reciprocal concept lines 50-58, 89-91 and 105-107 should explain that the merchant can retain Managed Payments as MoR for payments, fraud, disputes and transaction-level support when the seller remains responsible for all indirect-tax obligations. Managed Payments sends the tax-unsupported invoice in the seller's name and tax details, while sending a separate receipt email and PDF with Sold through Link details (old raw lines 133-157, new raw lines 136-161). This qualifies the how-it-works source lines 19-30 and November how-it-works lines 14-16 and 38-42: Link sends the communications, but sender and legal details displayed on the invoice are different fields. Seller-facing invoice settings configure the invoice details and do not control Link customer receipt dispatch.

Current source line 79 calls Stripe Tax a 'third-party tax solution', contradicting lines 59-61 and both captures (old raw lines 135-151, new raw lines 138-155). Stripe Tax is the only integrated tax solution compatible with Managed Payments. Optional third-party partners assist with registration, filing and remittance within the Stripe Tax workflow, which is different from an independent third-party tax provider integration. Zero additional Stripe Tax calculation fees on Managed Payments transactions do not imply that partner services, other Stripe services, taxes or a separate Stripe Tax deployment are free. Qualify index line 132 and Managed Payments concept lines 56 and 117. Stripe Tax concept lines 111-115 discusses other workflows and does not extend compatibility to Managed Payments.

Current source lines 28-33 and 53 mostly capture the domestic and cross-border rules but must keep the qualifying sales identity: Singapore-based seller to Singapore business customer self-identifying at checkout, all Japan-based seller domestic sales of digital goods, and Serbia only for cross-border sellers not registered for VAT in Serbia. Japan and Singapore also appear in the separate eligible cross-border destination list. The 82 unchanged entries are tax-coverage destination codes, not eligible seller locations, a complete supported customer list or evidence of an individual seller's account eligibility. Source lines 33 and 44 and Managed Payments concept line 54 undercount the listed codes. Both raw captures list 82 destinations, including 27 EU codes and conditional Serbia (old raw lines 19-131, new raw lines 20-134; separate November eligibility capture lines 5-24 and 70-103).

source_assessments.reason: The November capture adds a consequential threshold and responsibility explanation. Independently, the source overgeneralizes coverage, labels Stripe Tax as third-party, and omits the supported case where seller tax liability and Managed Payments merchant-of-record operations coexist.

answers.Q1: The November 7 capture of https://docs.stripe.com/payments/managed-payments/tax-compliance says Stripe handles indirect tax on covered digital-product sales in more than 80 countries, calculating and collecting tax where required, registering, filing, remitting and issuing tax invoices where required. Local volume and sales thresholds can produce taxability_reason: not_subject_to_tax in a covered country while Managed Payments still handles indirect-tax compliance (new raw lines 9-28). The seller is responsible for domestic sales by Japan-based businesses and Singapore domestic B2B sales, where the customer identifies as a business at checkout. Japan and Singapore appear in the cross-border list, and Serbia cross-border coverage applies only when the seller is not registered for VAT there (new raw lines 26-32, 46-75 and 121-134). Where Managed Payments cannot assume liability, the seller is responsible for local registration, calculation, collection, filing and remittance, even while Managed Payments can remain merchant of record for payments, fraud prevention, disputes and support. Stripe Tax is the only compatible integrated solution and adds no calculation fee for Managed Payments transactions. Registration and filing services can involve partners. Managed Payments sends a seller-identified tax invoice plus a separate receipt email and PDF with Sold through Link details. The seller keeps Invoice Settings current (new raw lines 136-161). The April 23 capture has the same country list and responsibility and document split, but lacks the November threshold paragraph (old raw lines 8-29 and 131-157). source-stripe-managed-payments-tax-compliance.md preserves much of that earlier scope but omits the continued MoR and Link receipt boundary and incorrectly calls Stripe Tax a third-party solution.
answers.Q2: At https://docs.stripe.com/payments/managed-payments/tax-compliance the substantive November documentation change is the threshold-based calculation example. A supported sale can carry taxability_reason: not_subject_to_tax while Stripe retains responsibility for indirect-tax compliance (old raw lines 19-25 and new raw lines 20-28). This outcome supplies no evidence of product or account eligibility, a jurisdiction's concrete threshold, a particular API object or version, or a general rule applying to every zero-tax result. Singapore buyer-to-customer terminology, Dashboard step numbering and invoice italics are presentation edits. The 82 listed cross-border destination codes do not change, including 27 EU codes and conditional Serbia (old raw lines 27-131 and new raw lines 30-134). Correct the approximate count and the EU subtotal in the current summary. Tax-coverage destinations are separate from supported seller locations. Keep April 23 evidence dated in source-stripe-managed-payments-tax-compliance.md, including Japan and Singapore domestic exceptions, the Serbia limitation, and the unsupported-transaction invoice identity. Qualify reciprocal Managed Payments, Stripe Tax and operations references. In unsupported tax cases, the seller owns registration, calculation, collection, filing and remittance while Managed Payments can remain merchant of record for operations. Stripe Tax is the sole compatible solution, and registration or filing partner support does not establish other integrated tax providers. The fee statement covers Stripe Tax calculations on Managed Payments transactions only. The invoice uses the seller's name and tax details, and separate emailed receipt and PDF use Sold through Link information (old raw lines 133-157 and new raw lines 136-161).
